question: IN GENERAL, which of the following sources of reduced vision may be associated with the condition depicted in the photo above?

options.A: this retinal condition is not associated with any type of vision loss

explanation: The photo depicts myelinated retinal nerve fibers (mRNFL). Remember, normal myelination of optic nerve fibers typically stops at the lamina cribosa before reaching the optic disc. However, in some cases, the myelination may extend anteriorly beyond the lamina cribosa resulting in retinal nerve fibers acquiring a myelin sheath. This anomaly results in the characteristic "feathery" white appearance of the retina that follows the orientation of normal retinal nerve fibers. Though typically an incidental and asymptomatic finding, myelinated retinal nerve fibers (in general) can actually result in reduced vision either from involvement of the macula, high myopia (not hyperopia), or ambylopia. In addition, it may be associated with nystagmus. (Editor's note: yes, we know that mNFL is generally an incidental finding without vision loss. We also acknowledge that the mNFL in the photo are not affecting the macula. However, the BCSC clearly states that mNFL can be associated with amblyopia) Comments: - I would word the question differently. "IN GENERAL", mNFL isn't associated with any vision loss (which you say in your editor's note) - this would make A also correct. It might better to say Which of the following can be associated etc... and leave out the IN GENERAL.

question: A 3-month-old girl with infantile spasms is referred to your clinic and has the following findings on fundus exam (see image). What abnormality is she mostly likely to have on further examination and workup?

options.A: Absence of the corpus callosum on MRI

explanation: This photograph depicts oval chorioretinal lacunae, the classic finding of Aicardi Syndrome. This is an X-linked dominant condition (i.e. lethal in males, except if person is XXY [Klinefelter] ), although the gene that causes this syndrome has not been identified as of 2012. The classic triad of Aicardi syndrome is chorioretinal lacunae, agenesis of the corpus callosum, and infantile spasms. Other ocular abnormalities include colobomas and microphthalmos. Infantile spasms typically develop before the age of 5 months and these individuals experience significant developmental delay. Answer "B" is referring to ocular toxocariasis which can commonly result in leucokoria (25%), localized macular granuloma (25%), or a peripheral granuloma (50%). Answer "C" is referring to Batten's disease which can result in optic atrophy, macular pigmentary deposits, and low/absent ERG. Patients with the different types of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Batten disease) can present with seizures, but typically a little later in life. Answer "D" is referring to neurofibromatosis type 2 whose classic findings are bilateral acoustic neuromas, cafe-au-lait spots (60%), combined retinal-RPE hamartomas, and posterior subcapsular cataracts. Comments: - AICardi Syndrome: Absence of corpus callosum Infantile spasms Chorioretinal lacunae OCULOPLASTY.

question: Compared to adult patients, which of the following is rare in pediatric patients with thyroid eye disease (TED)?
explanation: Thyroid eye disease (TED) is quite uncommon in children1 and tends to be more mild as compared to adult patients.2 Children with TED tend to have proptosis, eyelid retraction and lid lag, and soft tissue swelling (e.g. preorbital fat pad enlargement).2,3 However, unlike adults, extraocular muscle fibrosis and optic neuropathy are almost never observed.2,3 Antithyroid medications are the preferred initial and long-term treatment for TED.4 In severe cases refractive to medical management, subtotal thyroidectomy or radioiodine ablation may be required.4 It is important to discuss smoking cessation with adolescents or young adults who smoke as smoking is associated with more severe orbital disease.

question: A patient presents to your office with an abnormality of his inner canthi. You look up the abnormality in an atlas and find that it is called "dystopia canthorum." What syndrome is this abnormality specific for?
explanation: "Dystopia canthorum" describes the abnormality whereby the inner canthi and lacrimal puncti are displaced laterally. If one draws an imaginary line connecting the lower and upper puncti, this line will cross the cornea.

question: What is the proper definition of "ocular hypertelorism"?

options.A: increased distance between the inner canthi
options.C: increased distance between the medial walls of the orbits

explanation: Orbital hypertelorism is defined as excessive distance between the medial orbital walls as a result of lateralization of the orbits. This diagnosis is made radiographically. As an aside, telecanthus is defined as an increased distance between the inner canthi. It may be caused by hypertelorism. (Note: these terms are straight from the BCSC Pediatrics book) OTHER QUESTIONS.

question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this child?

options.A: globe exploration and repair in the operating room with simultaneous lensectomy due to disruption of the anterior capsule
options.B: globe exploration and repair in the operating room only
options.C: gluing of corneal wound and topical and systemic antibiotics
options.D: bandage contact lens and topical and systemic antibiotics

explanation: In young children, a fibrin clot can form quickly after penetrating trauma which can simulate liberated lens cortical material. It is not advisable to perform simultaneous lensectomy at the time of open globe exploration and repair unless you are completely certain that the anterior lens capsule is violated. In addition, even if the lens capsule is violated, it may be safer to perform lensectomy when the eye is more stable and less inflamed from the primary injury.

question: Which of the following statements regarding cerebral visual impairment (CVI) is correct?

options.A: Optic disc cupping can occur in preterm infants
options.B: CVI does not include subcortical visual impairment
options.C: Brain imaging is always normal in patients with CVI

explanation: Cerebral visual impairment (CVI), also termed retrogeniculate visual impairment refers to visual deficits resulting from pathology posterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus. CVI is also referred to as cortical visual impairment, but cerebral visual impairment is preferred because subcortical visual impairment can cause the same problems as those from cortical visual impairment. Neurological deficits may be present but it is possible that CVI is isolated. Some common causes include periventricular leukomalacia (a prominent cause of visual impairment in premature infants), intracranial hemorrhage, perinatal hypoxia, intrauterine infection, structural abnormalities, seizures, and hydrocephalus. Acquired causes include trauma (accidental and non accidental abusive), meningitis and encephalitis. On exam, patients with CVI have normal ocular structures, normal pupillary responses, but often have variable levels of visual inattentiveness. Parents and even the ophthalmologist may be uncertain as to the infant's ability to see. Nystagmus is typically not present. Although the retina exam is normal, subtle optic nerve changes may be present. Periventiruclar leukomalacia is most commonly associated with optic nerve changes such as optic nerve cupping (similar to glaucomatous cupping) in preterm infants. Workup includes neuroimaging, which may reveal changes such as periventricular leukomalacia, cerebral atrophy, porencephaly in the occipital cortex, etc. Often ERG results are normal while VEP results may be normal or subnormal. Comments: - Why don't many of these patients have a sensory nystagmus? - Nystagmus is thought to be from a pregeniculate visual impairment so pathology posterior to the LGN does not demonstrate nystagmus. Ocular structures are normal and sensory nystagmus probably stems from poor vision due to a structural deficit such as foveal hypoplasia.

question: Which of the following ocular tissues is most likely to be infiltrated by leukemia?
explanation: The retina and choroid are the most common ocular tissues infiltrated by leukemia. In fact by histology, the choroid is the most frequent involved ocular tissue, but its involvement is rarely seen clinically. Leukemia can infiltrate any ocular structure and ocular involvement is highly correlated with CNS leukemic disease. Leukemic retinopathy: • Most common ocular finding: retinal hemorrhages (especially flame-shaped in the nerve fiber layer). These retinal hemorrhages correlate with leukemia's other abnormalities of anemia, thrombocytopenia, and coagulation problems. • These hemorrhages may have white-centers and can look similar to those seen in shaken baby syndrome. Optic nerve infiltration: • May cause loss of central vision. • Translucent swelling of the disc obscures normal landmarks. • Can result in a white mass being seen over the optic disc in florid cases. • Disc edema + loss of central vision == medical emergency and these patients need radiation treatment as soon as possible. Anterior chamber infiltration: • Can lead to heterochromia iridis, iris infiltrates, spontaneous hyphemas, keratic precipitates, and pseudohypopyon. • Can lead to elevated intraocular pressure from the leukemic cells clogging the trabecular meshwork. • For iris involvement, may be confused with juvenile xanthogranuloma.

question: A 10-year-old girl is referred to your clinic for evaluation of proptosis. Her external appearance is shown in the photograph above. Mutations in what gene are responsible for this condition?
explanation: All known mutations that cause "Crouzon syndrome" affect the FGFR2 gene which is located on chromosome 10. Crouzon syndrome is the most common of the craniosynostosis syndromes. One helpful feature that distinguishes Crouzon from other craniosynostosis syndromes is the *lack* of syndactyly or brachydactyly in the former. Most craniosynostosis syndromes are autosomal dominant conditions. Briefly, here are the disease associations for the other answer choices: • TWIST -- Saethre-Chotzen syndrome • MYOC -- juvenile glaucoma, some POAG cases • OPTN -- normal tension glaucoma.

question: Of the following choices, which is considered to be the mildest craniosynostosis syndrome in terms of skull deformity?
explanation: Since the skull deformity in Saethre-Chotzen syndrome is quite mild, this syndrome often goes undiagnosed. It typically consists of plagiocephaly, ptosis, mild brachydactyly, and mild syndactyly. There is a characteristic lateral deviation of the big toes of the feet. This mild craniosynostosis syndrome is caused by mutations in the TWIST gene on chromosome 7. Crouzon is the most common autosomal dominant craniosyntosis. There is fusion of both coronal sutures leading to "tower skull". Intelligence is normal. The findings are limited to the skull unlike in Apert's. Apert's involves syndactyly of the hands and feet. Intelligence is often affected. Pfeiffer syndrome is another autosomally dominant craniosynostosis with syndactyly of the hands and feet but with characteristic short, broad thumbs and toes.

question: When premature closure of a cranial suture occurs, bone growth can only occur parallel to the suture line. What is the name of this bone growth pattern?
explanation: Craniosynostosis occurs when there is premature closure of 1 or more of the cranial sutures. When this occurs, bone growth cannot occur perpendicular to the suture line, but can still occur parallel to it. This bone growth pattern is called "Virchow's law".

question: You are examining a child on the Pediatric service with a past medical history of a "skull deformity" since birth. Based on your extensive reading, you suspect that the child has Apert syndrome. All of the following clinical features support your putative diagnosis EXCEPT:
explanation: Most of the craniosynostosis are autosomal dominant in inheritance. Patients with Apert syndrome typically have some mental deficiency, internal organ malformation (including cardiac), and a variety of abnormally-fused skull sutures. Syndactyly is a *prominent* feature of Apert syndrome and can result in the "mitten deformity" when all the digits are fused together. The one craniosynostosis syndrome that does *not* feature hand/feet/limb deformities is Crouzon syndrome.

question: What is the most common inheritance pattern with Alport Syndrome?
explanation: Alport syndrome is caused by a mutation(s) in basement membrane (collagen type IV) synthesis. It is characterized by glomerulonephritis, eye abnormalities, and hearing loss. Blood in urine (hematuria) is universal. The glomerulus of the kidney is heavily reliant upon a functional basement membrane as are the cochlea, retina, and lens capsule (also made of type IV collagen and a good way to remember Alport syndrome). Inheritance patterns: X-linked (85% of all cases): due to mutations in COL4A5 gene. high penetrance of hearing loss in affected males high-tone sensorineural deafness by age 20 (other tones progressively lost later in life) dot and fleck retinopathy occurs in 85% of adult males anterior lenticonus occurs in 25% retinopathy and lenticonus generally are not present until adulthood posterior polymorphous dystrophy is also associated with Alport syndrome autosomal recessive: due to mutations in COL4A3 and COL4A4 genes. autosomal dominant (very rare): also due to mutations in COL4A3 and COL4A4 genes neurosensory hearing loss heriditary hematuric nephritis lenticular changes (anterior lenticonus, spherophakia, cataracts) arcus juvenilis whitish yellow retinal lesions Prior to genetic testing being readily available, any patient with a family history of Alport syndrome and a dot and fleck retinopathy was to be considered "diagnostic" for having Alport syndrome. Patients suspected of having Alport Syndrome are now sent for genetic testing confirmation. "Oil droplet" cataracts refer to the appearance of the lens' red reflex by retinoscopy. It has the appearance of a small oil drop in the middle of the lens. See the reference picture A in the link below. ?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=4386265_CJN.10581014f3. jpg Posterior lenticonus will also give an oil droplet cataract. Posterior lenticonus is almost always unilateral and is a type of congenital cataract. The anterior lenticonus seen in Alport Syndrome is generally bilateral and occurs later in life (acquired and not congenital). Galactosemia also produces an oil droplet cataract but it occurs within the first few weeks of life. The nucleus and deep cortex become opacified and cause the oil droplet appearance by red reflex. Treatment involves elimination of milk from the diet. Galactosemia is screened for at birth by law and lethal within a few weeks if not treated. Another interesting note is that certain mutations causing Usher Syndrome (congenital sensorineural hearing loss and retinitis pigmentosa) have genes that code for basement membrane as well.

question: Which of the following disorders is associated with myelinated nerve fibers (of the optic nerve)?
explanation: Basal Cell Nevus Syndrome (Gorlin-Goltz Syndrome) is an uncommon autosomal dominant, multi-systemic disorder characterized by multiple basal cell carcinomas, skeletal abnormalities, odontogenic keratocyst, and intracranial calcification. Myelinated nerve fiber layer is common with this disorder. Myelinated nerve fiber layers can be associated with neurofibromatosis 1, ipsilateral high myopia, strabismus, and amblyopia.

question: What is the name given to the cranial malformation that occurs when there is premature closure of the skull base suture?
explanation: Premature fusion of the skull base suture produces only one kind of abnormality called "midface hypoplasia". Abnormal fusion of the calvarial sutures (e.g. coronal, sagittal, etc) can produce a variety of skull malformations (e.g. plagiocephaly, scaphocephaly, etc). Here are the definitions from BCSC: Hypertelorism, ocular: excessive interpupillary distance when compared to standard nomograms. It implies orbital hypertelorism which is excessive distance between the medial orbital walls. Telecanthus: Greater than normal distance between the medial canthi. This can be secondary to hyperterlorism, or it can be a primary soft-tissue abnormality. Craniosynostosis: premature closure of 1 or more cranial sutures during the embryonic period or early childhood. Premature suture closure prevents perpendicular growth but allows parallel growth along the closed suture. So if the sagittal suture is closed, then the head will be long; and if the coronal suture is closed, then the head is flat and will be wide. Plagiocephaly: most common form of craniosynostosis, or most commonly seen in a pediatric ophthalmology practice. In a child with unilateral coronal suture synostosis, one will find that on the synostotic side, the forehead and supraorbital rim are depressed or recessed, the interpalpebral fissure is wider, and the orbit is often higher. The nonsynostotic side displays a protruding or bulging forehead, a lower supraorbital rim, a narrower interpalpebral fissure, and frequently a lower orbital position. Brachycephaly: result of bilateral closure of the coronal sutures, resulting in a wide and flat forehead. Scaphocephaly: result of premature closure of the sagittal suture, resulting in a long head. Midface hypoplasia: result of fusion of the sutures at the skull base. This will not change the forehead region (cranium) but cause facial deformations. Here, one sees maxillary hypoplasia, beak-shaped nose, shallow oribts with proptosis and lagophthalmos, high-arched palate, and a prominent-appearing jaw.

question: Which of the following craniosynostosis is most commonly associated with syndactyly?
explanation: Craniosynostosis is the premature closure of 1 or more cranial sutures during the embryologic period or early childhood. Common systemic features of the craniosynostosis syndrome include fusion of multiple calvarian sutures and skull base sutures. Crouzon syndrome is generally not associated with syndactyly at all. It is however, the most common autosomal dominant craniosynostosis. The Crouzon’s phenotype has been linked to over 30 mutations of the FGFR2 gene on chromosome 10. Seathre-Chotzen syndrome is a much milder craniosynostosis . It is often under- diagnosed, due to the mild features of the syndrome. Intelligence is usually normal and only occasionally do these patients display slightly short digits of their hands and feet. Apert syndrome, resembles Crouzon syndrome, except the former displays an often extreme amount of syndactyly. Oftentimes, Apert’s syndrome patients have completely fused hands and feet. Most patients with this syndrome also have one of two specific mutations of the FGFR2 gene. Pierre Robin sequence, is technically not a craniosynostosis and also not associated with syndactyly. It is a frequent finding in Stickler syndrome. Comments: - Fingers and toes cant be moved "Apert" from each other.
